callouts.label: Whole Grains
callouts.hint: The oats, barley, brown rice, and whole-grain bread grouped along the left edge.
callouts.description: Oats, barley, brown rice, and whole-grain bread add four plant foods and provide different fibers and resistant starches.
callouts.ap_tip: Plant variety includes grains; it is not limited to fruits and vegetables.

callouts.label: Colorful Vegetables
callouts.hint: The broccoli, red cabbage, carrot, and spinach in the upper-left corner.
callouts.description: Broccoli, red cabbage, carrot, and spinach contribute four distinct plant types with varied fibers and phytochemicals.
callouts.ap_tip: Color can be a useful variety cue, but no single color or vegetable is required.

callouts.label: Mucus Layer
callouts.hint: The translucent blue-green coating just inside the upper-left colon wall.
callouts.description: A mucus layer separates much of the microbial community from the intestinal epithelium and contributes to barrier function.
callouts.ap_tip: The microbiome lives in a structured habitat; microbes are not simply mixed evenly throughout the gut.

callouts.label: Whole Fruits
callouts.hint: The apple, pear, orange, and blueberries across the upper center.
callouts.description: Apple, pear, orange, and blueberries add four more plant types and a mixture of pectins, other fibers, and polyphenols.
callouts.ap_tip: The poster counts plant types, not servings or a required prescription.

callouts.label: Fermentable Plant Fiber
callouts.hint: The tan strands woven through the microbes in the upper part of the lumen.
callouts.description: Some carbohydrates resist digestion in the small intestine and reach the colon, where microbial communities can ferment them.
callouts.ap_tip: Different fiber structures can support different microbial functions; variety changes the available substrates.

callouts.label: Microbial Diversity
callouts.hint: The dense central ecosystem of rods, spheres, chains, clusters, curves, and spirals.
callouts.description: The gut microbiome contains many organisms with different shapes, genes, and metabolic roles. The image is an artistic ecosystem view, not a species-identification chart.
callouts.ap_tip: In the American Gut observational study, participants reporting more than 30 plant types per week differed in microbial diversity from those reporting 10 or fewer; the result is an association, not proof that one target causes health outcomes.

callouts.label: Legumes
callouts.hint: The black beans, chickpeas, and green lentils at the upper-right edge.
callouts.description: Black beans, chickpeas, and green lentils add three plant types rich in fermentable carbohydrates, fiber, and protein.
callouts.ap_tip: Different varieties of beans and lentils can count as different plants in a diversity tally.

callouts.label: Nuts
callouts.hint: The almonds, walnuts, pistachios, and peanuts grouped on the right.
callouts.description: Almonds, walnuts, pistachios, and peanuts contribute four plant types along with fiber, fats, protein, and phytochemicals.
callouts.ap_tip: Peanuts are botanically legumes, but they still represent a distinct plant food in the weekly variety count.

callouts.label: Seeds
callouts.hint: The chia, flax, and pumpkin seeds in the lower-left cluster.
callouts.description: Chia, flax, and pumpkin seeds add three compact plant types with distinct fibers, fats, minerals, and polyphenols.
callouts.ap_tip: Small quantities of herbs, spices, nuts, and seeds can broaden variety without requiring a large portion of each.

callouts.label: Spices
callouts.hint: The turmeric root, cinnamon sticks, and black peppercorns at the lower-left edge.
callouts.description: Turmeric, cinnamon, and black pepper add three more plant sources and show how spices can contribute to dietary diversity.
callouts.ap_tip: A diversity goal can include culturally meaningful seasonings rather than prescribing one cuisine.

callouts.label: Gut Epithelium & Barrier
callouts.hint: The folded pink cell layer along the inner lower-left wall of the colon.
callouts.description: A single epithelial cell layer helps separate the intestinal contents from the body while transporting water and selected nutrients.
callouts.ap_tip: Barrier function depends on cells, mucus, immune activity, microbes, diet, and many other factors—not one food alone.

callouts.label: Short-Chain Fatty Acids
callouts.hint: The small glowing gold and blue droplets near the lower-center colon wall.
callouts.description: Microbial fermentation can produce short-chain fatty acids such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate. These molecules participate in local gut metabolism and signaling.
callouts.ap_tip: Butyrate is an important fuel for colon cells, but production varies with microbes, substrates, transit, and other conditions.

callouts.label: Microbial Genes & Resistome
callouts.hint: The DNA-like loops and plasmid forms inside microbes at center-right.
callouts.description: Gut microbes carry genes that shape their functions, including antibiotic-resistance genes collectively called the resistome.
callouts.ap_tip: The American Gut study observed lower abundance of selected antibiotic-resistance genes in the group reporting more than 30 plant types; it did not establish a simple causal mechanism.

callouts.label: Alliums
callouts.hint: The garlic bulb and red onion at the lower-right edge.
callouts.description: Garlic and red onion add the final two plant types in this illustrated set of 30 and contain fermentable fructans for many people.
callouts.ap_tip: Tolerance differs; people with digestive conditions may need individualized guidance rather than maximizing every fermentable food.

callouts.label: Fresh Herbs
callouts.hint: The parsley, basil, and cilantro leaves along the lower-right side.
callouts.description: Parsley, basil, and cilantro contribute three plant types and demonstrate that herbs can count toward variety.
callouts.ap_tip: The 30 pictured foods span vegetables, fruits, legumes, grains, nuts, seeds, herbs, spices, and alliums.
